summary: Defines a way to carry one IP datagram as the payload inside another IP datagram. This is useful for tunneling, such as delivering traffic to a mobile device that is away from home.

plainLanguage.summary: IP-in-IP places an IP datagram inside a second IP datagram. The outer address takes it to a tunnel endpoint, which removes the outer header and forwards the original packet.

why use encapsulation instead of ip source routing

subtitle: A way to carry an IP datagram inside another IP datagram to steer it through a tunnel.

tldr.problem: Normal IP routing may not send a datagram through an intermediate node that can deliver it to its final destination.
tldr.mechanism: An encapsulator adds an outer IPv4 header addressed to a tunnel exit. The exit removes that header and forwards the original datagram.
tldr.outcome: IP-in-IP offers an alternative to source routing, with additional header overhead. RFC 2003 has been updated by RFC 3168 and RFC 6864.

today: RFC 2003 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 3168 and RFC 6864.

sections.title: How IP Encapsulation Works
sections.content:
RFC 2003 specifies how one IP datagram can be carried as the payload of another. The outer header sends the packet to an intermediate destination that normal routing would not select from the original destination address.

At the tunnel exit, the outer header is removed and the original datagram is delivered toward its destination. The entry and exit points are the tunnel endpoints. The source, entry, exit, and destination can all be separate nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender adds an IP header that directs a packet to an intermediate endpoint. That endpoint removes the added header and forwards the original packet.

sections.title: Why Use Encapsulation
sections.content:
The RFC describes Mobile IP as one use: an agent can receive a datagram for a mobile node and deliver it at the node's current location. Other possible uses include multicasting, policy routing, and choosing routes with selected security attributes.

Encapsulation can be preferable to the IP loose source route option because routers and firewalls may handle source-routed packets poorly, and source routing raises security and authentication concerns. The trade-offs are that encapsulated datagrams are typically larger and the tunnel exit must be able to decapsulate them.
sections.plainLanguage: Encapsulation can steer traffic without changing its original destination address. It adds packet size and requires a tunnel endpoint that can remove the added header.

sections.title: The Outer and Inner Headers
sections.content:
The encapsulator inserts an outer IPv4 header before the original header. The outer source and destination identify the tunnel endpoints; the inner addresses retain the original sender and recipient. The outer Version and Protocol fields are 4, and the Type of Service value is copied from the inner header.

The inner header is otherwise unchanged during the tunnel trip. If encapsulation is part of forwarding, its TTL is reduced by one. An encapsulator MUST NOT send an inner datagram with TTL zero, and a decapsulator MUST discard an inner datagram whose TTL is zero after removal of the outer header.
sections.plainLanguage: The outer header names the tunnel endpoints, while the inner header keeps the original addresses. The inner packet's TTL is reduced when the encapsulator is forwarding it.

sections.title: Handling Tunnel Errors
sections.content:
A router inside a tunnel may send an ICMP error to the encapsulator. When the returned packet contains enough information, the encapsulator can remove the outer header and relay a suitable error to the original sender. Datagram Too Big errors MUST be relayed; some errors must not be relayed because their meaning would be wrong for the original packet.

ICMP routers are only required to return 8 octets beyond the IP header, which may not include the inner header. The RFC therefore recommends that encapsulators keep soft state about a tunnel's MTU, path length, and reachability so they can report useful errors when later packets violate that state.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel entry point receives errors from the network and decides which ones make sense to report to the original sender. It keeps tunnel information because an error may not include the original packet header.

sections.title: MTU and Fragmentation
sections.content:
Encapsulators MUST support Path MTU Discovery soft state inside tunnels. When reporting an MTU to the original sender, the encapsulator SHOULD account for the outer header size. The RFC generally prefers fragmenting the original packet before encapsulation to fragmenting the encapsulated packet, because the latter requires reassembly at the tunnel exit.

Implementations MUST use at least one method described in the RFC for managing MTU mismatches. Options include adjusting source packet sizes, fragmenting before encapsulation, or fragmenting the resulting tunnel packet where appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel adds header bytes, so a packet that fit before may exceed the path's size limit. Encapsulators must support a way to handle this mismatch.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Encapsulation can make filtering harder because the original addresses, protocol, and transport ports are no longer in their usual positions. Routers that filter traffic need to account for encapsulation, and the RFC warns that unauthenticated encapsulated packets can create significant security risks.

Hosts that receive encapsulated datagrams SHOULD accept only traffic that is harmless, comes from a trusted authenticated source, contains an IP Authentication header inside, or is addressed to the decapsulator or a node with a special relationship to it. Router checks should be a backup to checks by the receiving host.
sections.plainLanguage: The outer header hides some details that network filters normally inspect. Hosts should accept encapsulated packets only when they meet the trust conditions described in the RFC.
